chapters.title: One. The Pans
paragraphs: Ines walked out to the salt pans before the sun was up. She liked the hour when the water was still and the herons stood like posts.
The pans stretched to the dunes in long white squares. Each square had a wooden rake beside it and a heap of salt drying at one corner.
Ines picked up the first rake. She drew it slowly through the brine, and the crust broke into small grey plates.
By six the other workers had come down the dyke. They called greetings across the water and set to work without hurry.
Duarte arrived last, as he always did. He carried the bread and the flask and set them on the sluice gate.
The work went on until the light turned hard. Nobody talked much once the heat came.
Ines stopped at noon to drink. She looked along the dyke towards the town and saw the carts already waiting.
Duarte came over with the flask. He poured two cups and handed one across without a word.
The salt was good that year. The merchants said so, and the prices said so too.
In the afternoon the wind turned off the sea. The heaps crusted over, and the rakes were laid down in a row.
Ines counted the heaps twice. She wrote the number on a slate and hung the slate on the gate.

chapters.title: Two. The Carts
paragraphs: The carts came down the salt road at dusk, six of them in a line. The drivers walked beside the mules and sang to keep them steady.
Duarte loaded the first cart himself. He lifted each sack onto his shoulder and swung it up with a grunt.
Ines checked the slate against the sacks. She found one sack short and sent a boy back to the pans for it.
The road to the town was narrow and rutted. The carts creaked and rocked, and the mules flicked their ears at the flies.
At the toll bridge the keeper came out with a lantern. He counted the carts, took the coins and waved them through.
Duarte rode on the last cart with his legs hanging over the tail. He whistled the same tune over and over until Ines laughed.
The town was still awake when they reached it. Lamps burned in the windows above the square.
The merchant met them at the warehouse door. He weighed every sack and wrote the weights in a ledger.
Ines watched the scales closely. She had learned long ago that a merchant's thumb was heavier than it looked.
When the last sack was weighed, the merchant paid in silver. Duarte bit one of the coins, and everyone laughed.
They drove the empty carts home under the stars. The road was quiet, and the sea was a long pale line beyond the dunes.
